Introduction:
In England, each year, respiratory pathogens circulating in the community, particularly SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), place strain on healthcare systems. In winter 2023–4, there were 96.6, 76.9, and 37.8 cumulative admissions per 100 000 people in England for COVID-19, influenza, and RSV, respectively [ 1 , 2 ]. Public health and healthcare leaders better use scarce resources when they can predict hospital admissions and bed occupancy, reallocating staff and beds to elective care as emergency admissions decline.

Forecasting gives quantitative assessments of future events, harnessing historic trends and modeled assumptions. However, infectious disease dynamics are challenging to confidently understand in real time due to their partial observation and complexity. When used well, numerical forecasts help to inform healthcare planning to allocate resources more effectively, improving health outcomes. Within England, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) is responsible for the prevention, preparation, and response to infectious diseases; National Health Service England provides healthcare; and both are overseen by the Department of Health and Social Care.

Influenza forecasts have been produced over many years in the USA by the Centre for Disease Control [ 3 , 4 ]. Forecasting is not limited to influenza; challenges cover West Nile virus [ 5 ], Ebola [ 6 ], and chikungunya [ 7 ], with collaborations between government and academia driving methodological improvements [ 8 , 9 ]. These methods and initiatives were enhanced during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic response [ 10 , 11 ] and communicated publicly.

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic disrupted seasonal patterns of many respiratory viruses, driven by population-mixing dynamics impacted by control interventions [ 12 ], limiting influenza and RSV transmission. As population mixing returned to pre-pandemic levels, these diseases reemerged in winter 2022–3 [ 13 ]. Rising emergency hospital admissions due to influenza, COVID-19, and RSV place direct resource pressure on hospitals [ 14 ]. These admissions require inpatient beds and the increased hospital demand reduces the planned and nonemergency care available. Therefore, accurate prediction of infectious disease pressures helps to manage the wider healthcare system.

Multiple metrics are used to understand seasonal respiratory disease waves, tackling different policy questions: peak magnitude, peak timing, cumulative incidence, and incidence over time [ 4 ]. Comparisons between rapid collections and retrospective records give confidence in our choice of metrics for real-time modeling [ 15 ]. In addition, we focus on test-positive diagnoses to ensure that modeling is specific to a pathogen, allowing us to model diseases separately [ 16 ].

Over the winter 2023–4 season, UKHSA delivered a forecasting model suite to estimate hospital admissions and bed occupancy of COVID-19, influenza, and RSV. The breadth of pathogens and metrics modeled was key to the utility of the suite. The forecasts were used directly to inform national policy discussions and integrated into regional-level decision-making. In this work, we outline our approach in delivering this forecasting suite, key considerations, and describe our real-time results.
Methods:
### Data sources

The National Health Service is a publicly funded healthcare system that covers England, shown spatially in Supplementary Figure S1 , with consistent data collection across hospitals [ 17 ]. Individuals presenting severe symptoms of an infectious disease are often tested in secondary care settings, with diagnostic tests reported to UKHSA via the Second-Generation Surveillance System (SGSS). There is high ascertainment and coverage of SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV testing in hospitals for differential diagnoses. However, this ascertainment can vary with demographics such as age [ 18 ] and clinical setting [ 19 ]. More broadly, all-cause hospitalizations can be predicted by seasonal patterns and environmental effects [ 20 ]. However, infectious disease presentations are less predictable, particularly when seasonal transmission patterns are disrupted. Test-positive hospitalizations, admissions, and bed occupancy are key metrics for the pressures sustained by hospitals due to infectious disease. Forecast target definitions are provided ( Table 1 ), highlighting their differences.

### Forecast models

Our modeling suite focuses on statistical forecasts, following evidence of their strong performance in short-term forecasting tasks relative to strictly mechanistic approaches [ 21 , 22 ]. Alongside their predictive performance, this class of models are fast, largely disease-agnostic, and do not require substantial historic data. Furthermore, we developed model ensembles that capture uncertainty in possible trends [ 23 ], with evidence of improved performance [ 24 , 25 ]. Model ensembles also reduce our reliance on individual models, improving operational resilience.

In an M -open model combination, for possible candidate models M , we ideally have a breadth of modeling approaches to produce combination estimates [ 26 ]. However, practical considerations are critical in ensemble design. Across pathogens and metrics, there is a single-day turnaround from modeling to dissemination, highlighting the importance of speed and reliability. Candidate models are selected if the model:

Criterion (i) makes the production of all forecasts feasible, allowing error flagging, model reruns, and the thorough assurance of results. While models can be run in parallel, there are limitations on how many individuals are available to run the process, make fixes, and quality-check results. Criterion (ii) ensures desirable qualities for ensembling and the coherence of prediction aggregations, such as from local to national levels. Criterion (iii) is a holistic evaluation of model performance and utility. Models are not selected by scoring rules alone, but instead we consider the wider properties of a model (reliability, ease of use, difference from existing models) and discussion with surveillance experts.

A variety of statistical models were deployed—each model is structured separately for each disease, adapted to reflect the surveillance data being modeled, with key hyperparameters retuned regularly over the season. The primary model class used was a generalized additive model (GAM), which uses the semi-mechanistic assumption of a recent growth rate extrapolated forward in time [ 27 ] via the mgcv and gratia packages [ 28 , 29 ]. To improve model performance, we leverage probabilistic population catchment areas, with hospital population sizes attributed by the proportion of historic admissions resident in each administrative region, to define a denominator population for hospital admissions [ 30 ]. Secondly, we use state-space-based models, such as Error Trend Seasonality (ETS) structures, fitted to the time series of each individual geographic location via the fable package [ 31 ]. Lastly, syndromic surveillance is regressed to predict future admissions given current leading indicator levels [ 32 ]. Each week, models are first inspected by the team (applying expert judgment) and then candidate models are ensembled. Supplementary Table S1 outlines the models by disease, with model structures outlined in Supplementary Section 1 .

For COVID-19 and influenza, in addition to admissions, we forecast beds occupied with test-positive patients, requested by users. A convolution is fitted between the admissions and occupancy time series, estimating time to discharge, translating the admissions forecast into an occupancy forecast.

To compare models and tune parameters, we use probabilistic scoring—primarily the weighted interval score, interval coverage, and bias, via the scoringutils [ 33 ] R package. Prediction intervals of 90% and 50% are generated, with the 90% interval and median communicated to users, alongside probabilistic statements assessing trends. While quantitative scoring is a key component in developing our ensemble, within-team expert judgment is necessary to exclude models weekly.

Unweighted average quantile ensemble approaches are widespread in epidemic forecasting [ 34 , 25 ]. Instead, we preserve individual model sample predictions [ 35 ] and then perform an unweighted quantile summary of draws across all models. This captures uncertainty in a granular way when summarizing predictions, avoiding averaging or aggregating point estimates.

A prediction sample approach requires higher data volume than point estimates; however, as modeling is within one team, this has limited impact. By using a prediction sample stacking approach, we produce granular forecasts at local levels and then aggregate the sample draws to higher geographies, allowing simple reconciliation across space, time, and other quantities of interest (such as age for RSV) [ 36 ]. Our users need national forecasts and fine-scaled geographies – their coherence is important for credibility.

Lastly, the use of prediction samples allows us to assign probabilities to different interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, and decrease) by using thresholds agreed with disease and operations experts at all geographies. We consider a change over 2 weeks of <20% to be stable, a positive change of >20% as an increase, and a negative change of >20% as a decrease, similarly to approaches worldwide [ 37 ].
Results:
In a time of disrupted and uncertain seasonal patterns caused by the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we chose to forecast our metrics over a forecast horizon window, showing how the metric is expected to develop. As a trade-off between long forecast horizons with high uncertainty and short horizons with lower utility, we chose a consistent 14-day horizon across all models. This provides enough foresight to be useful, with meaningfully small uncertainty, agreed with end users of the forecasts.

### Season overview and targets

Each disease is monitored differently across the healthcare system, with varying granularity and quality. The forecast targets selected are given in Table 1 , with further detail in Supplementary Table S2 . A key consideration for target choice is latency, traded off against accuracy. For operational efficiency, forecasts for each disease were not delivered every week of the winter. Forecasts were prioritized based on the trends observed and stopped early if needed; new models were incorporated and further metrics were included as the season progressed. The timeline of metrics forecasted over the season are given in Figure 1 .

Our confidence in each data stream and what is interesting to users vary by disease, so the spatial-resolution modeled is inconsistent across diseases. COVID-19 admissions have the highest quality of reporting due to their priority during the pandemic, though age information is not captured. Alternatively, as RSV individual data are processed by UKHSA, models stratified by age are possible.

### Influenza

The seasonal influenza epidemic in 2023–4 was characterized by a small peak before the New Year and a second larger peak afterwards ( Figure 2 ). Observed 14-day admissions and occupancy values were within the forecasted 90% prediction intervals in 15/19 and 10/11 weeks, respectively, though the admissions forecast performed poorly between peaks ( Figure 2 ). For influenza, the GAM was included in the ensemble across all weeks, the ETS model was incorporated later in the season, and leading indicator models were used intermittently.

### COVID-19

Unlike those for influenza, COVID-19 admissions were at non-zero levels at the start of winter, with multiple peaks and troughs observed in admissions and occupancy trends ( Figure 3 ). The main peak occurred near the New Year. The COVID-19 forecasts have variation in their accuracy, with forecasts generally struggling in growth/decline phases, when the models are slow to adapt to changing trends ( Figure 4 ). Of the five available models for the ensemble, none were used across all weeks. The GAM was used most frequently, with sporadic use of leading indicator models, and the ETS model was consistently deployed later in the season.

### RSV

Relative to influenza and COVID-19, the peak in the RSV epidemic was earlier in the season, occurring in November ( Figure 4 ). All but two of the 14-day forecasted 90% prediction intervals contain the observed values, capturing the trend in the epidemic well across the wave. One single model was used—a GAM with age and regional stratifications.

### Forecast performance

Quantitative evaluation of forecast accuracy is critical to the communication and improvement of forecasts. Performance breakdowns show varying skill across diseases, metrics, and geographies ( Table 2 ). Across 90% and 50% coverages, the regional forecasts were better calibrated than their national aggregations. The occupancy forecasts for COVID-19 and influenza had better-performing central estimates than the corresponding admissions forecasts due to the slower evolving trend.

Forecast performance varies over time ( Figure 5 ) as the epidemics change phase. The COVID-19 Weighted Interval Score are more consistent over time than the influenza and RSV metrics, which score poorly near the peak. Further scoring metrics and regional breakdowns are explored in Supplementary Tables S3–S5 . The national quantile forecasts for the ensemble and individual models are given in Supplementary Figures S2–S4 .
Discussion:
This manuscript describes the UKHSA’s modeling approach for delivering a suite of forecasts across three priority diseases in the 2023–4 winter season. Forecasts harnessed the unified data collection of healthcare in England, giving high hospital coverage, low latency, and granular spatiotemporal resolution. Some forecasts were particularly accurate, such as RSV admissions ( Figure 4 ). However, modeling for COVID-19 admissions was challenging during this season ( Figure 2 ). The forecasts were widely disseminated within the health system, with modelers and operations colleagues collaborating closely. The resulting forecasts had high utility at national and regional geographies, aiding resource allocation decisions.

Forecast users ranged from senior ministers responsible for the nation’s health to regional health protection teams, with a variety of use cases in between ( Figure 6 ). National forecasts were shared weekly with the Department of Health, supporting ministerial oversight. This aided system performance decisions and operating policy. At a subnational level, forecasts were discussed at weekly regional operational meetings in NHS England. This gave foresight for regional decision-makers on hospital capacity, operational pressure [ 38 ], and the coordination of mutual aid. Additionally, regional health protection teams used the products to anticipate pressure on public health responses.

An in-house approach allowed UKHSA modelers to leverage existing relationships between disease experts and data collectors to develop useful forecasts. Granular, unified data collection enabled geography-specific forecasting, directly supporting local operations and further strengthening cross-system relationships. By developing models within a single team, the creation of new targets and experimentation with new approaches were straightforward, which is critical for future outbreaks. By focusing on statistical time-series methods, the suite can be scaled to new diseases and metrics without the challenging parameterization of mechanistic approaches. The sample-based ensembling can be applied with many model types, providing reconciliation across spatial scales and trend categorization, aiding decision-making.

The modeling suite was developed iteratively over the past 3 years. Beginning in 2021 with a single COVID-19 model, winter 2022–3 evolved into a COVID-19 ensemble and influenza forecast. In 2023–4, we created ensembles for COVID-19 and influenza, with an RSV forecast added. This development over time allowed adaptation to evolving user needs, methodological experimentation, and efficiency improvements over the summer. However, there is room for accuracy improvement. COVID-19 models performed better regionally compared with nationally for interval coverage—due to trend-pooling assumptions. The strong performance of influenza short-term forecasting gives us confidence in the methods for winter 2024–5, though more approaches should be investigated. Exploration of different trend-pooling assumptions in multiscale epidemics is an important avenue for future research.

Forecasts were not delivered to stakeholders over the 2-week holiday period ( Figure 1 )—weeks with high system burden. This decision was made based on capacity and changes to data reporting (delay and frequency). Human decision-making is still required to provide effective epidemic forecast ensembles and quality assurance is critical to maintain trust with users.

The target choice underpins forecast utility, particularly the horizon length. Statistical models have excelled at short horizons relative to longer time periods [ 22 ]. Our work has a short-term focus, with a 14-day look ahead, providing reasonable uncertainty in trends. We have found that the 2-week horizon is highly useful for stakeholders, with meaningful uncertainty, though longer horizons would allow for more planning. Medium-term-scenario modeling, in which academic collaborations have excelled and mechanistic models are utilized [ 39 ], has a different purpose to the immediate decision-making of short-term forecasting.

The extensions to this modeling suite are clear: improvements in forecast accuracy, incorporation of mechanistic assumptions, new disease targets, and further granularity. To improve timeliness, joint nowcasting and forecasting should be considered to harness lagged data. The current suite of models is primarily statistical, deploying models with more mechanistic components, further disease dynamics assumptions, and the incorporation of historical trends are avenues for exploration [ 40 ]. Other diseases should be considered for forecasting, creating the capability for responsive modeling work and giving broader system pressures. Increased sharing of data and code would benefit methods development and assurance, though we must be careful that this does not limit modelers’ agility to deliver in response periods, and flexibility to try new targets and metrics. The open sourcing of forecast targets to the UKHSA Data Dashboard would enable more effective collaboration, particularly in an outbreak. Working with patient identifiable data does introduce risk in open-sourcing work, though a refactoring of current operational code could facilitate this change.

A key insight shared from this work and used by customers is the use of probabilistic trends. In future seasons, these should be robustly evaluated. Furthermore, the use of additional scoring metrics could strengthen the model evaluation, such as log-transformations as recommended [ 41 ]. Probabilistic scoring is key to assessing accuracy, although this is only one component of model evaluation. Assessing model fits and validating their performance against simulated epidemics, past waves, and epidemic phases could improve robustness and avoid overfitting.

Modeling in-house only, largely due to data-sharing challenges, limits the public availability of forecasts in real time. The closed source work limits the scrutiny and collaboration available for the project. Furthermore, by focusing efforts within a team, there is limited capacity for novel model development. This means that academic expertise is not being directly leveraged to inform predictions—though the team does engage in the forecasting community. Barriers prevent government modelers from deploying novel methods developed in academia. Newly developed models should clearly state runtimes, be validated on multiple spatial scales and waves, and be well documented and evaluated by using proper scoring rules against sensible baseline models.

The ensemble is limited by a lack of mechanistic dynamic components, such as susceptible depletion, which could improve performance at epidemic turning points. Incorporating mechanistic assumptions or past-season data could improve predictive performance for seasonally driven diseases such as influenza and RSV. These assumptions come at the cost of adaptability to new epidemic waves, as past seasons may not be representative of future waves. This season, we prioritized rapid operational delivery, with statistical methods and a short-term horizon at the expense of modeling full disease dynamics, due to customer demand.

Over the 2023–4 winter season, we delivered a forecasting suite for respiratory disease hospitalizations in England with a range of statistical and ensemble models. These model outputs were used widely across the health system for situational awareness and supported decision-making at national and local levels. We have shown that having an internal capability for real-time modeling of infectious diseases supports the delivery of effective public health.
